semesters.title: Semester 1
semesters.description: Networking basics, switching, IPv4, services, security, and a small-office capstone.

semesters.title: Semester 2
semesters.description: Switching, wireless, routing, and first-hop redundancy lessons are planned.

semesters.title: Semester 3
semesters.description: Enterprise networking, security, automation, and WAN lessons are planned.

modules.title: Modules 1-3: Networking Today, Basic Switch and End Device Configuration, Protocols and Models
Modules 4-7: Physical Layer, Number Systems, Data Link, and Ethernet Switching
Modules 8-10: Network Layer, Address Resolution, and Basic Router Configuration
Modules 11-13: IPv4 Addressing, ICMP, and Transport Layer
Modules 14-15: Application Layer and Network Services
Modules 16-17: Network Security Fundamentals and Build a Small Network

steps.prompt: Before touching the topology, predict which device forwards frames between PC1, PC2, and SRV1, and which devices are endpoints.
hints: Endpoints create or consume data; infrastructure forwards it.
A switch does not usually originate user traffic in this lab.
steps.commandCoach: No commands yet. Say the path out loud: PC1 sends an Ethernet frame to SW1, and SW1 forwards it toward the destination.
steps.explanation: The switch is the LAN forwarding device. PCs and servers are endpoints because they create, receive, and respond to application traffic.

steps.prompt: Cable PC1 eth0 to SW1 FastEthernet0/1. Watch the link lights and decide why both ends matter.
hints: Use cable mode, then click PC1 and SW1.
Pick the Ethernet port on each side if the simulator asks.
steps.commandCoach: No IOS command is needed. Physical connectivity is the first layer of the story.
steps.explanation: Layer 1 must be present before Ethernet, ARP, IP, or application traffic can work. Both interfaces need a usable cable and an up state.

steps.prompt: Finish the small LAN by cabling PC2 and SRV1 to SW1, then inspect how the topology changed.
hints: Keep PC2 on FastEthernet0/2 and SRV1 on FastEthernet0/3 for the cleanest assessment.
If you used a different switch port, remove the cable and try the suggested port.
steps.commandCoach: Topology edits are the learning action here. Think: what changed at Layer 1 and Layer 2?
steps.explanation: Every endpoint now has a path to the switch. The switch can learn each endpoint MAC address after traffic begins.

steps.prompt: Send a packet or ping from PC1 to 192.168.10.12. Notice that no router is required inside one IPv4 subnet.
hints: Open PC1 and ping PC2's address.
Same-subnet traffic goes through the switch, not a default gateway.
steps.commandCoach: From PC1, use ping 192.168.10.12.
steps.explanation: PC1 and PC2 share 192.168.10.0/24, so PC1 resolves PC2's MAC with ARP and sends the frame directly through SW1.

lessons.title: IOS Modes and Hostname Muscle Memory

steps.prompt: Predict which IOS mode lets you change a switch hostname: user EXEC, privileged EXEC, global configuration, or interface configuration.
hints: Show commands mostly live in EXEC modes.
Changes to the running configuration live under configure terminal.
steps.commandCoach: The command path is enable, configure terminal, hostname ACCESS1.
steps.explanation: Hostname is a global setting, so it belongs in global configuration mode.

steps.prompt: Rename SW1 to ACCESS1 from the CLI.
hints: Enter privileged EXEC with enable.
Use configure terminal, then hostname ACCESS1.
steps.commandCoach:
enable
configure terminal
hostname ACCESS1
steps.explanation: The prompt changes because the running configuration changed. The hostname becomes part of the device identity in every prompt and config export.

steps.prompt: Give ACCESS1 a management address on VLAN 1: 192.168.10.2/24.
hints: A switch management IP goes on an SVI, not a physical access port.
Use interface vlan 1, ip address 192.168.10.2 255.255.255.0, no shutdown.
steps.commandCoach:
interface vlan 1
ip address 192.168.10.2 255.255.255.0
no shutdown
steps.explanation: An SVI gives a Layer 2 switch an IP identity for management. It does not turn the switch into a router.

steps.prompt: Save the running configuration so the switch would keep it after a reload.
hints: Running config is active now; startup config survives reload.
Use copy running-config startup-config or write memory.
steps.commandCoach:
end
copy running-config startup-config
steps.explanation: The running configuration is in RAM. Saving creates startup configuration so the intended state persists across reloads.

steps.prompt: Predict what happens if a correct cable is present but a router interface is administratively down.
hints: Physical cable is necessary but not always sufficient.
Administrative state is a local software decision.
steps.commandCoach: You will fix the port with interface configuration in the next step.
steps.explanation: A link can fail because of cabling, interface compatibility, power, or administrative shutdown. Link state is the combined result.

steps.prompt: Cable R1 GigabitEthernet0/0/0 to SW1 FastEthernet0/24.
hints: Use an Ethernet cable between router and switch.
The exact ports matter for this lesson's check.
steps.commandCoach: No command yet. Build the physical path first.
steps.explanation: Routers and switches can connect over Ethernet. The cable gives the devices a chance to exchange frames once both ports are up.

steps.prompt: Bring R1 GigabitEthernet0/0/0 up from the CLI.
hints: Use interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0.
The command that reverses shutdown is no shutdown.
steps.commandCoach:
enable
configure terminal
interface gigabitEthernet 0/0/0
no shutdown
steps.explanation: The no shutdown command clears the administrative down state. Data-link protocols can operate only after the interface is administratively enabled.

steps.prompt: Explain the difference between physical connectivity and administrative state in one sentence.
hints: One is about the medium; one is about configured intent.
A perfect cable still fails when the interface is shut down.
steps.commandCoach: No extra command. Use the Events panel and link markers as evidence.
steps.explanation: Physical connectivity gives a signal path; administrative state tells the device whether it is allowed to use that path.

lessons.title: ARP and MAC Learning in Motion

steps.prompt: Predict what SW1 does with the first frame from PC1 before it has learned the destination MAC address.
hints: Switches learn source MAC addresses.
Unknown unicast and ARP requests are flooded inside the VLAN.
steps.commandCoach: The simulator packet trace will make the prediction visible.
steps.explanation: A switch learns from source MAC addresses. If the destination is unknown or broadcast, it floods the frame out other ports in the VLAN.

steps.prompt: Ping PC2 from PC1 and watch ARP happen before the ICMP echo succeeds.
hints: The first ping may create ARP events first.
Open the packet inspector if you want the protocol breakdown.
steps.commandCoach: From PC1, use ping 192.168.10.12.
steps.explanation: PC1 must know PC2's MAC address before it can send the IPv4 packet in an Ethernet frame.

steps.prompt: Put SW1 FastEthernet0/1 and FastEthernet0/2 in access VLAN 10.
hints: Use interface range FastEthernet0/1-2.
Access ports carry one data VLAN for normal endpoint traffic.
steps.commandCoach:
interface range fastEthernet 0/1-2
switchport mode access
switchport access vlan 10
steps.explanation: Both endpoints now share VLAN 10. Switching and ARP stay inside that broadcast domain.

steps.prompt: Ping PC2 again. Notice that same-VLAN traffic still works after the access VLAN is explicit.
hints: If the ping fails, confirm both ports are in VLAN 10.
A same-subnet pair must also be in the same VLAN.
steps.explanation: IPv4 addressing and VLAN membership must line up. Same subnet plus same VLAN gives the hosts a direct Layer 2 path.

steps.prompt: Predict why PC1 needs a default gateway to reach PC2 when they are in different IPv4 networks.
hints: A host compares the destination IP to its own subnet mask.
Off-subnet traffic is sent to a router interface.
steps.commandCoach: You will give R1 one interface in each LAN.
steps.explanation: A host uses its default gateway when the destination is outside its local prefix. The gateway is the router interface on the local LAN.

steps.prompt: Configure R1 GigabitEthernet0/0/0 as PC1's gateway: 192.168.10.1/24.
hints: Use interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0.
Do not forget no shutdown.
steps.commandCoach:
interface gigabitEthernet 0/0/0
ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
no shutdown
steps.explanation: R1 now has an IPv4 identity in PC1's network and can receive frames addressed to its router MAC.

steps.prompt: Configure R1 GigabitEthernet0/0/1 as PC2's gateway: 192.168.20.1/24.
hints: The second LAN uses 192.168.20.0/24.
Each routed interface must be in a different subnet.
steps.commandCoach:
interface gigabitEthernet 0/0/1
ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
no shutdown
steps.explanation: R1 is directly connected to both LANs. It can now route between them if hosts point at the correct gateways.

steps.prompt: Ping PC2 from PC1. Explain why the packet uses R1 even though both PCs are nearby on the canvas.
hints: Topology distance on the canvas is not the same as IP network distance.
The subnet mask decides local vs remote.
steps.commandCoach: From PC1, use ping 192.168.20.12.
steps.explanation: PC1 sends the frame to R1's MAC because 192.168.20.12 is outside PC1's /24. R1 then forwards toward the 192.168.20.0/24 LAN.

steps.prompt: Predict what would happen to interface IP addresses after a reload if you only changed running-config.
hints: Running-config is active now.
Startup-config is read at boot.
steps.commandCoach: The persistence command comes at the end.
steps.explanation: Unsaved running-config changes are lost after reload. Startup-config is the durable boot source.

steps.prompt: Rename R1 to EDGE1 so every later prompt and log message identifies the edge router clearly.
hints: Hostname is global configuration.
Use hostname EDGE1 from config mode.
steps.commandCoach:
enable
configure terminal
hostname EDGE1
steps.explanation: A useful hostname makes logs, prompts, topology diagrams, and troubleshooting less ambiguous.

hints: If you already did this in the previous lesson, the checks may complete quickly.
The hostname changed, but the interface names did not.
steps.commandCoach:
interface g0/0/0
ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
no shutdown
interface g0/0/1
ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
no shutdown
steps.explanation: Router interface addresses are the anchor points hosts use as default gateways.

steps.prompt: Save EDGE1's running configuration.
hints: Exit to privileged EXEC or use do copy from config mode if supported.
write memory is accepted too.
steps.commandCoach:
end
copy running-config startup-config
steps.explanation: Saving is a professional habit: it converts a working moment into a reproducible device state.

steps.prompt: Predict why PC1 cannot reach PC2 when R1 and R2 both know only their directly connected networks.
hints: A router forwards only when the route table has a matching destination.
Connected networks do not automatically teach a neighbor.
steps.commandCoach: You will add one route on each router.
steps.explanation: Each router needs a route to the remote LAN. Without one, the packet is dropped even when links are physically healthy.

steps.prompt: On R1, add a static route to 192.168.20.0/24 through R2 at 10.0.0.2.
hints: The destination is the remote LAN, not the next-hop link.
The next hop is R2's address on the 10.0.0.0/30 link.
steps.explanation: A static route says: for this destination prefix, forward packets to this next-hop address.

steps.prompt: On R2, add the return static route to 192.168.10.0/24 through R1 at 10.0.0.1.
hints: Packets need a path there and a path back.
Return traffic fails without the reverse route.
steps.explanation: Two-way communication needs forwarding knowledge in both directions unless a default route or dynamic protocol covers one side.

steps.prompt: Ping PC2 from PC1 and connect the success to both routers' route tables.
hints: If it fails, check both static routes and both PC gateways.
A ping reply must return to the source network.
steps.explanation: The echo request follows R1's route to R2. The echo reply follows R2's route back to R1.

steps.prompt: Choose a smart test order: local gateway, next router, remote gateway, then remote host. Why that order?
hints: Troubleshooting gets easier when each test narrows the fault domain.
Start close, then move outward.
steps.commandCoach: The ping target changes as the scope expands.
steps.explanation: A layered test sequence tells you where the path stops instead of only proving that the final target failed.

steps.prompt: From PC1, ping its local default gateway 192.168.10.1.
hints: This tests PC1 IP settings, cabling, VLAN, and R1's LAN interface.
If local gateway ping fails, remote tests are noise.
steps.explanation: The local gateway test confirms that PC1 can reach the first routing hop.

steps.prompt: From PC1, ping R2's LAN gateway address 192.168.20.1.
hints: This test crosses the router-to-router link.
If it fails after local gateway works, focus on routes or the transit network.
steps.explanation: Reaching the remote gateway proves the inter-router path works before testing the final host.

steps.prompt: Now ping PC2 at 192.168.20.12 and explain what changed from the previous test.
hints: The last segment is R2 to PC2.
If only this fails, check PC2 addressing or its switch link.
steps.explanation: The final test includes every segment: PC1 LAN, R1, transit link, R2, and PC2 LAN.

lessons.title: DHCP Gives Hosts a Starting Point

steps.prompt: Predict the minimum DHCP information a host needs to communicate off its local network.
hints: An address alone is not enough for remote networks.
Think IP address, mask, gateway, and often DNS.
steps.commandCoach: The pool will carry network, default-router, and dns-server values.
steps.explanation: A useful DHCP lease includes an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS server so users do not configure hosts manually.

steps.prompt: On R1, exclude 192.168.30.1 through 192.168.30.20 from DHCP assignment.
hints: Routers, servers, and printers often use reserved addresses.
Excluded addresses stay out of dynamic leases.
steps.commandCoach: ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.30.1 192.168.30.20
steps.explanation: Exclusions protect addresses used for infrastructure or static assignments.

steps.prompt: Create DHCP pool LAN30 with network 192.168.30.0/24, default router 192.168.30.1, and DNS server 192.168.30.10.
hints: The network line defines the address pool.
The default-router option should be the LAN interface on R1.
steps.commandCoach:
ip dhcp pool LAN30
network 192.168.30.0 255.255.255.0
default-router 192.168.30.1
dns-server 192.168.30.10
steps.explanation: The pool turns network policy into a repeatable lease offer for every DHCP client on that LAN.

steps.prompt: Use DHCP on PC1, then ping R1 at 192.168.30.1.
hints: Open PC1 and request DHCP from its desktop or CLI.
If the lease fails, confirm the pool and R1 interface.
steps.commandCoach: On PC1, use dhcp or the IP configuration app's DHCP action, then ping 192.168.30.1.
steps.explanation: The host receives addressing information from R1, then proves local IP connectivity to the default gateway.

lessons.title: DNS and HTTP: Names Become Sessions

steps.prompt: Predict which happens first when a user opens http://intranet.openpt: DNS resolution or the HTTP request.
hints: HTTP needs a destination IP before TCP can connect.
DNS maps the name to an address.
steps.commandCoach: You will configure the name and then prove reachability.
steps.explanation: The client resolves the name first, then starts a transport session to the returned IP address.

steps.prompt: Ensure SRV1 uses 192.168.30.10/24 with default gateway 192.168.30.1.
hints: A service endpoint still needs normal IP settings.
The server gateway points to R1's LAN address.
steps.explanation: Servers need stable addresses so DNS records and clients have a dependable target.

steps.prompt: On R1, add a host record mapping intranet.openpt to 192.168.30.10.
hints: This simulator uses the router host table as the simple DNS-style name source.
Use ip host name address.
steps.commandCoach: ip host intranet.openpt 192.168.30.10
steps.explanation: A name record lets learners think in service names while the network still forwards to IP addresses.

steps.prompt: From PC1, ping intranet.openpt or 192.168.30.10, then explain where DNS stops and HTTP would begin.
hints: If name lookup is not available in the current tool, ping the IP and explain the name step.
Application protocols depend on working lower layers.
steps.explanation: DNS provides the destination IP. ICMP proves reachability; HTTP would then use transport and application-layer exchanges with the same server address.

steps.prompt: Predict why a network admin should prefer SSH over Telnet for remote management.
hints: Think confidentiality and authentication.
Remote management crosses networks you may not fully trust.
steps.commandCoach: SSH needs a domain name, local user, RSA keys, SSH version, and VTY transport.
steps.explanation: SSH encrypts the management session. Telnet sends the session in clear text.

steps.prompt: On SW1, set ip domain-name openpt.local and create username admin secret class123.
hints: The domain name participates in SSH key generation.
Use a local username for login.
steps.commandCoach:
ip domain-name openpt.local
username admin secret class123
steps.explanation: Local credentials and a domain name prepare the device for SSH server operation.

steps.prompt: Generate RSA keys on SW1 and force SSH version 2.
hints: If the simulator accepts the default modulus, the checker expects 2048.
SSH version 2 is the modern baseline.
steps.commandCoach:
crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
ip ssh version 2
steps.explanation: RSA keys give the SSH server cryptographic identity. SSHv2 avoids older protocol behavior.

steps.prompt: Restrict SW1 VTY lines 0 through 4 to SSH only.
hints: VTY lines are remote terminal lines.
Use line vty 0 4, then transport input ssh.
steps.commandCoach:
line vty 0 4
transport input ssh
steps.explanation: Restricting VTY transport closes the Telnet path and keeps remote management on SSH.

steps.prompt: Turn on service password-encryption and save SW1's configuration.
hints: This is not the same strength as SSH, but it avoids casual clear-text display.
Save after security changes.
steps.commandCoach:
service password-encryption
end
copy running-config startup-config
steps.explanation: Basic hardening layers small controls: encrypted management, limited transports, local users, and saved known-good configuration.

steps.prompt: Predict a good build order for a small office: cables, interface IPs, routes/services, security, or testing first?
hints: A later layer depends on earlier layers.
Testing happens throughout, but final proof comes after configuration.
steps.commandCoach: Use the order: physical, interface addressing, services, security, proof.
steps.explanation: Good network work is staged. Each checkpoint narrows the next possible failure.

steps.prompt: Cable PC1 to SW1 F0/1, PC2 to SW1 F0/2, SRV1 to SW1 F0/3, and SW1 F0/24 to R1 G0/0/0.
hints: Use the specified switch ports so later assessment stays predictable.
Bring R1's interface up after the cable exists.
steps.commandCoach: Topology first. CLI comes next.
steps.explanation: The cabling plan creates a single LAN behind a router. Port choice makes troubleshooting and documentation easier.

steps.prompt: Configure R1 G0/0/0 as 192.168.50.1/24 and bring it up.
hints: The router interface is the default gateway for this office LAN.
Remember no shutdown.
steps.commandCoach:
interface g0/0/0
ip address 192.168.50.1 255.255.255.0
no shutdown
steps.explanation: The default gateway anchors the LAN and gives hosts a way to leave the subnet later.

steps.prompt: Ping R1 from PC1 at 192.168.50.1.
hints: PC1 must have an IP in 192.168.50.0/24 and gateway 192.168.50.1.
If it fails, check the cable, PC addressing, and R1 interface state.
steps.explanation: This proves the endpoint, switch port, router interface, and IP subnet agree.

steps.prompt: Plan the office build in four checkpoints: physical, addressing, services, security. What will you test after each checkpoint?
hints: Good builders create proof points before moving on.
Each test should isolate one kind of failure.
steps.commandCoach: Write the tests in your head before you configure: link state, gateway ping, service ping, saved security.
steps.explanation: The capstone rewards a disciplined build loop: predict, configure, test, explain.

hints: Use static endpoint addressing here to keep the final proof deterministic.
steps.commandCoach: On R1: interface g0/0/0, ip address 192.168.50.1 255.255.255.0, no shutdown. On endpoints, set IP, mask, and gateway.
steps.explanation: The LAN now has an addressing plan with a router gateway, user hosts, and a stable server.

steps.prompt: On R1, add ip host intranet.openpt 192.168.50.10 so the office has a memorable service name.
hints: Names reduce cognitive load for users and admins.
The network still forwards to an IP address.
steps.commandCoach: ip host intranet.openpt 192.168.50.10
steps.explanation: A service name connects the application layer to the addressing plan.

steps.prompt: Harden SW1 for SSH: domain openpt.local, user admin secret class123, RSA keys, SSHv2, and VTY SSH only.
hints: Reuse the SSH hardening pattern from the earlier mission.
VTY lines control remote CLI access.
steps.commandCoach:
ip domain-name openpt.local
username admin secret class123
crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
ip ssh version 2
line vty 0 4
transport input ssh
steps.explanation: Security is not an afterthought. It is part of the final definition of done for a working network.

steps.prompt: Prove the office works: ping SRV1 from PC1 at 192.168.50.10, then save the router and switch configurations.
hints: The ping proves service reachability at the network layer.
Saving proves the working state can survive a reload.
steps.commandCoach: From PC1: ping 192.168.50.10. On R1 and SW1: copy running-config startup-config.
steps.explanation: You have built, tested, secured, and persisted a small office network. That is the Semester 1 loop in miniature.
